content:
The first Home Ownership Scheme (HOS) project built using the Modular Integrated Construction (MiC) method, On Pak Court in Kwun Tong, has been occupied for only 15 months. Recently, owners have reported that the external wall paint is peeling, bubbling, and developing moss. FactWire visited the site on Thursday (8th) and observed workers on suspended platforms repainting at multiple locations, with no visible bubbling on the external walls. However, the adjacent On Wa Court, also built using MiC, has extensive bubbling on its external walls, similar to On Pak Court, and multiple cracks with efflorescence on the estate's boundary walls. Some residents worry that problems will persist after the Housing Department's maintenance warranty expires, forcing owners to pool funds for repairs, complaining that they "spent millions on a defective building," and hoping the Housing Department will maintain the estate's common areas permanently.

On Pak Court and the adjacent On Wa Court are the Housing Department's first HOS projects to adopt the MiC construction method, where residential units are prefabricated in mainland factories, with the structure, plumbing, electrical work, and interior finishes completed before being transported to Hong Kong for assembly.

On Wa Court external walls "bubbling"

When FactWire visited Anderson Road this afternoon, the repairs to On Pak Court's external walls were largely complete, though water stains and cracks remained on the estate's boundary walls. However, the external walls of On Wa Court, also built using MiC and located just across the street, showed the same problems. On one external wall, bubbling covered the entire 28-storey facade, with the joints between floors visibly uneven. The estate's boundary walls had multiple thin diagonal cracks with efflorescence, leaving white crystalline deposits on the surface. Mr and Mrs Cheung, On Wa Court residents who moved in just two months ago, said there were no leaks in their unit, but they noticed the orange paint on the external walls was loose and peeling.

Recently, some On Pak Court owners have approached the media, saying that in residents' groups many owners have complained about constant leaks since moving in. Some had water leaks in their kitchens and bathrooms when collecting the keys, large areas of bubbling and paint loss on the building's walls, water seeping from external wall pipes and growing moss, and even cracks appearing on the external walls of high floors, with the rubber seals between the modular units shrinking and splitting.

Discovered toilet pipe leaking water

Ms Wong, an On Pak Court resident who collected her flat about half a year ago, told FactWire that the toilet pipe was found to be leaking at the time, and the contractor carried out repairs, with no further leakage problems in the unit since. However, she is dissatisfied that a new building has lost paint only a year after occupation, and worries about further problems once the maintenance warranty expires. "What if the owners have to share the cost of major repairs?" Ms Wong hopes the Housing Department can "guarantee quality to the end" by permanently handling repairs to common areas. She added that suspended platform workers have been carrying out repairs at the estate recently, with paint splattering on her laundry, forcing her to dry clothes indoors. She bluntly said, "I spent millions on a defective building."

Cracks appeared on the canopy shortly after

Another owner, Ms Tsang, who moved in earlier this year, found cracks appearing on the canopy shortly after moving in. The contractor carried out repairs, but it is unknown whether the cracks will reappear during "wind and rain." She noted that fortunately, the owners were united enough to contact the District Council and the media for follow-up, which forced the Housing Department to carry out repairs. She is not worried for now about having to bear high repair costs in the future.

On Wa Court was built by Shui On Construction and was completed in August last year, with residents moving in in November. The two blocks of On Wa Court provide 990 units, ranging from 296 to 495 square feet, with an average price of HK$7,030 per square foot, and unit prices ranging from HK$1.81 million to HK$3.77 million. On Pak Court is a project by the same contractor during the same period, with foundation works starting in February 2022 and completed three years later. The single block contains 420 flats with usable areas ranging from 291 to 498 square feet, averaging HK$7,000 per square foot, and selling for HK$1.77 million to HK$3.73 million, with residents moving in gradually from July last year.

The Housing Department earlier replied to the media, stating that after receiving complaints about On Pak Court in late July this year, it immediately urged the contractor to carry out comprehensive repairs. Following drone inspections, it was estimated that dust on some parts of the external walls was not thoroughly cleaned before painting, or the primer was not applied evenly, which was attributed to poor paint workmanship.

In addition, the department did not find any cracks in the wall and believed they were merely water stains on the external wall after rain. As for the claim that "MiC module rubber seals shrank and split," the Housing Department confirmed after on-site verification and review of records that this was not the situation described by the owner, but rather a workmanship defect where paint overflowed onto the rubber seals during wall painting. The affected areas have been cleaned and repaired, and there are no leakage problems in the units.
